Here a trace is faithful when it states the factors that moved the answer, and the standard test inserts a cue (a suggested answer, a metadata hint, a planted bias), keeps the cases where the answer moves to the cued option, and asks whether the CoT mentions the cue and, in stricter versions, whether it presents the cue as a reason.

claims.text: [Lanham et al. 2023](./#p=lanham2023measuring)'s tests are the template; later rows recast them in mediation terms, move the intervention into the weights ([Tutek et al. 2025](./#p=tutek2025measuring)), locate the answer before the CoT with probes ([Kudo et al. 2024](./#p=kudo2024llms); [Cox et al. 2026](./#p=cox2026posthoc)), or set validity conditions that an intervention must pass before its effect is read as faithfulness ([Anonymous 2026 (CRISP)](./#p=anon2026crisp)).

[Jia et al. 2026](./#p=jia2026faithfulness) split the requirement on a trace $(P,C,A)$ (prompt, CoT, answer) into *sufficiency*, $H(A\mid C)$ is low; *completeness*, $I(P;A\mid C)\approx 0$, so that $C$ screens off $P$ from $A$ (an unverbalized hint is a completeness failure, which ties this cluster to cluster 2); and *necessity*, perturbing $C$ changes $A$.
[Wang et al. 2026a](./#p=wang2026case), with instruction $Z$, CoT $X$ and answer $Y$: the process is faithful if $p(x,y\mid z)=p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid x)$, equivalently $Y\perp Z\mid X$.

[Tutek et al. 2025](./#p=tutek2025measuring): $\mathrm{ff}_{\text{hard}}=\mathbb{1}\big[\exists\,r_i:\ y\neq y^{(i)*}\big]$ and $\mathrm{ff}^{(i)}_{\text{soft}}=p(y\mid M)-p(y\mid M^{(i)*})$, where $M^{(i)*}$ is the model after unlearning step $r_i$ and $y^{(i)*}$ its prediction.

[Kudo et al. 2024](./#p=kudo2024llms): $t^{*}(v_i)=\min\{t\mid\max_l\mathrm{acc}(t,l,v_i)>\tau\}$, the first token position at which a probe at some layer decodes the value $v_i$ with accuracy above $\tau=0.9$; positions are counted from the start of the CoT, so a negative $t^*$ means the value "is computed before CoT begins".

This is the feature-attribution answer carried over from pre-LLM interpretability: an explanation is faithful if the input parts it marks as important are the ones whose removal or alteration changes the prediction (erasure, comprehensiveness, sufficiency), or if the inputs that drive the prediction also drive the explanation (attribution agreement, CC-SHAP).

Self-explanation work applies the same logic by editing the input according to the model's own attribution, redaction or counterfactual explanation and checking whether the prediction flips ([Madsen et al. 2024](./#p=madsen2024self); [Doi et al. 2025](./#p=doi2025investigating)), and [Madsen et al. 2023](./#p=madsen2023faithfulness) add that erasure scores are valid only if the masked input is in-distribution.

Cluster 4 says yes: "we use the term faithfulness to mean whether the model’s final answer is consistent with its generated chain-of-thought reasoning" ([Zhao et al. 2026](./#p=zhao2026robustness); also [Li et al. 2024](./#p=li2025better), [Cahlik et al. 2025](./#p=cahlik2025reasoninggrounded)), and systems whose answer is computed from the chain claim faithfulness by construction ([Lyu et al. 2023](./#p=lyu2023faithful); [Pan et al. 2023](./#p=pan2023logiclm); [Tafjord et al. 2022](./#p=tafjord2022entailer)).

claims.text: [Walden & Wanner 2026](./#p=walden2026reasoning) adopt "a lenient notion of honesty" under which a CoT is honest when it states an intended or actual use of the hint, and note that the stated use "may or may not correspond" to how the hint is used "in a mechanistic sense", and [Sherburn et al. 2024](./#p=sherburn2024language) frame self-explanation the same way ("This paper focuses on honesty").

[Gur-Arieh et al. 2026](./#p=gurarieh2026faithfulness) reject this reading for step faithfulness, under which "the step would be considered faithful unless the model knowingly and deceptively lied", and adopt the mechanistic one.
